messages.subject: Kolmogorov-Smirnov
parts:
Hi All,

I am confused. I am getting two different answers for something I suppose should be the same:

Example:

x=c(6,4,3,1,9,4,1,4,7,2,6,2,7,6,1,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,5,1,55)

y=c(6,4,3,1,9,4,1,4,5,2,1,2,3,6,1,5,4,1,2,5,1,2,5,1,5)

find ks distance from seewave library:


ks.dist(x, y,f = 1)$D

> ks.dist(x, y,f = 1)$D
[1] 0.327083


now find ks distance using ks.test from stats
> ks.test(y, x,f = 1)

 Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  y and x
D = 0.16, p-value = 0.9062
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

Can any one help me understand why D is different in the two cases?
Thanks,

messages.author: de80047cbc18c87e
messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Kolmogorov-Smirnov
parts:
Hello,

This is because ks.dist() scales each spectrum to be compared by its
integral (probability mass function). With your data:

x <- c(6,4,3,1,9,4,1,4,7,2,6,2,7,6,1,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,5,1,55)
y <- c(6,4,3,1,9,4,1,4,5,2,1,2,3,6,1,5,4,1,2,5,1,2,5,1,5)
x.pmf <- x/sum(x)
y.pmf <- y/sum(y)
# the two following lines are equivalent
ks.test(x.pmf, y.pmf)$statistic
ks.dist(x, y)$D

HTH

Jerome

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Kolmogorov-Smirnov -- additional information
parts:
Hello again,

Sorry this is not the full right explanation. I replied too quickly
(not fully awaken).

The function ks.dist() takes as input two spectra that are a kind of
distribution functions. These distribution functions are then scaled
by their integral to obtain probability mass functions. The distance D
is computed on the difference between the cumulative distribution
functions.

The KS test for unpaired samples takes as input two unordered raw data
and then computes the distance D (statistic) on their respective
cumulative distribution functions.

It is then expected that ks.dist()$D and ks.test()$statistic differ,
it was actually the motivation of writing ks.dist().

Sorry if I added confusion and hoping to be now really awaken,

HTH

Jerome
